title: There is / there are - existence
shortExplanation: There is a park. There are five rooms.
longExplanation:
The construction there is/are means “exists/exist”, “is”.
• There is + singular noun. number
• There are + plural noun. number
Negation: There isn't / There aren't
Question: Is there...? / Are there...?
formation: There is a park. There are five rooms.

examples.sentence: There is a cinema near here.
Are there any shops nearby? — Yes, there are.
examples.translation: Are there any shops nearby? - Yes.

title: Prepositions of place: in, on, at, under, next to, behind, between
shortExplanation: in the box, on the table, at the station
longExplanation:
Three main prepositions:
• in = inside something: in the box, in the city, in bed
• on = on the surface: on the table, on the wall, on the left
• at = at a specific point: at the station, at home, at school
Others: under (under), next to/beside (near), behind (behind), in front of (in front), between (between), opposite (opposite)
formation: in the box, on the table, at the station

examples.sentence: The keys are on the table.
examples.translation: The keys are on the table.

title: Imperative
shortExplanation: Open your books. Don't run. Please sit down.
longExplanation:
Imperative = base form of a verb without a subject.
Negation: Don't + infinitive
Please makes the request politer (at the beginning or end).
To include the speaker: Let's + infinitive → Let's go! Let's eat!
formation: Open your books. Don't run. Please sit down.

title: can / can't - skill and resolution
shortExplanation: I can swim. She can't drive. Can I help you?
longExplanation:
can is a modal verb, expresses:
1. Skill/Ability: I can play the guitar
2. Opportunity: It can be dangerous
3. Resolution (spoken): Can I use your phone?
formation: I can swim. She can't drive. Can I help you?

title: Question words: what, where, who, when, how, why, which, whose, how much/many
shortExplanation: What is this? Where do you live? How old are you?
longExplanation:
Question words appear at the beginning of the question, followed by an auxiliary verb before the subject.
• what = what/which
• where = where/where
• who = who (question without do: Who lives here?)
• when = when
• why = why
• how = how; how much = how many (uncountable); how many = how many (count); how old = how old; how long = how long
formation: What is this? Where do you live? How old are you?

examples.sentence: How many brothers do you have?
examples.translation: How many brothers do you have?

title: Quantitative numerals: 1–1000
shortExplanation: one, two, three... twenty-one, a hundred, a thousand
longExplanation:
Numerals 1–12: special words (one, two, three... twelve).
13–19: + -teen (thirteen, fourteen... nineteen; exceptions: thirteen, fifteen, eighteen).
Tens: twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety.
Compounds: 21 = twenty-one (via hyphen).
100 = a/one hundred; 1000 = a/one thousand.
After hundred/thousand - and (BrE): two hundred and fifty.
formation: one, two, three... twenty-one, a hundred, a thousand

examples.sentence: The ticket costs four hundred pounds.
examples.translation: The ticket costs four hundred pounds.

title: Ordinal numbers: first, second, third...
shortExplanation: the first, the second, the third, the fourth... the twenty-first
longExplanation:
Ordinal numbers are formed by adding -th: fourth, fifth, sixth...
Exceptions: first (1st), second (2nd), third (3rd), fifth (5th), eighth (8th), ninth (9th), twelfth (12th).
Always used with the article the: the first day, the third floor.
Fractions: ½ = a half, ⅓ = a third, ¼ = a quarter.
formation: the first, the second, the third, the fourth... the twenty-first

examples.sentence: My office is on the third floor.
examples.translation: My office is on the third floor.

examples.sentence: Today is the first of March.
examples.translation: Today is the first of March.

title: Possessive case: 's and s'
shortExplanation: John's car, my sister's friend, the children's toys, the teachers' room
longExplanation:
In English, belonging is expressed by an apostrophe + s:
• Singular: Tom's book, the dog's tail
• Plural with -s: apostrophe only: the teachers' room, my parents' house
• Irregular plural: 's: the children's playground, men's clothes
• Names ending with -s: James's / James' - both options are correct
formation: John's car, my sister's friend, the children's toys, the teachers' room

examples.sentence: The children's toys are in the box.

title: Prepositions of movement: to, into, out of, up, down, along, across, through
shortExplanation: go to school, walk into the room, run across the street
longExplanation:
• to = direction to a point: go to work, walk to the park
• into = movement inward: come into the room, jump into the pool
• out of = movement outward: get out of the car, take out of the bag
• up/down = up/down: climb up the hill, walk down the stairs
• along = along: walk along the river
• across = across/through: swim across the lake, walk across the road
• through = through: drive through the tunnel
formation: go to school, walk into the room, run across the street

title: Past Simple - regular verbs: +ed
longExplanation:
Past Simple - a completed action in the past with or without a specific tense.
Rules for writing the ending -ed:
• Most verbs: + ed → worked, played
• End in -e: + d → loved, used
• Consonant + -y: -y → ied → studied, tried
• One vowel + one consonant (short stressed syllable): double the consonant → stopped, planned

title: Past Simple - irregular verbs (table)
longExplanation:
About 200 irregular verbs need to be learned by heart. The most frequent 50 cover ~90% of uses.
Groups by similarity of changes:
• AAA (do not change): cut, put, hit, set, let
• ABA (return to the beginning): run→ran→run, come→came→come
• ABC (all different): go→went→gone, be→was/were→been

examples.sentence: I went to Paris last summer.
examples.translation: I went to Paris last summer.

title: Past Simple - negation: didn't + infinitive
shortExplanation: She didn't go (not: didn't go). I didn't see him.
longExplanation: Negation: didn't (= did not) + infinitive for all persons.
formation: She didn't go (not: didn't go). I didn't see him.

examples.translation: She didn't show up for work.

title: Past Simple - questions: Did you? Where did she go?
shortExplanation: Did they arrive? What did he say?
longExplanation:
Question: Did + subject + infinitive?
Special questions: Where/When/What + did + subject + infinitive?
formation: Did they arrive? What did he say?

title: was / were - verb to be in the past
longExplanation:
Past tense of the verb to be:
• was - with I, he, she, it
• were - with you, we, they
Negation: wasn't / weren't
Question: Was she...? Were they...?

examples.sentence: I was very tired last night.
examples.translation: I was very tired last night.

examples.sentence: They were at home all day.
examples.translation: They were at home all day.

title: will - predictions and spontaneous decisions
shortExplanation: I'll call you back. It will rain tomorrow. I'll have the pasta.
longExplanation:
will is used for:
1. Spontaneous decisions (made at the time of speech): I'll help you with that.
2. Predictions without a specific plan: I think it will rain.
3. Promises: I won't tell anyone.
4. Requests: Will you open the window?
Abbreviation: 'll. Negation: won't (= will not).
formation: I'll call you back. It will rain tomorrow. I'll have the pasta.

examples.sentence: The phone is ringing. — I'll get it!
examples.translation: The phone is ringing. - I will answer!
